description: We are a team of passionate students interested in space, technology, and problem-solving.  Our goal is to learn, collaborate, and build a meaningful project that addresses a real-world challenge.
summary:
Problem. Climate change is experienced locally, yet long-term trends are hard to see in raw monthly data, and it is easy to mistake natural variability for a real signal.

Solution. Earth System Trend Detective analyzes 35 years of NASA POWER data and presents the results in an interactive map and dashboard. Each location is classified as increasing, decreasing, or showing no significant trend, based on a Mann-Kendall test at the 5 percent significance level. Sen’s slope gives the rate of change, and yearly anomaly charts with a fitted trend line show how each place has changed over time.

Rigor. The analysis was run over two time windows, 1990-2025 and 2000-2025, and the app flags which results remain the same in both. This separates robust findings from fragile ones.

Findings. Rainfall shows a significant increase at the large majority of locations across both periods. Temperature trends are mixed, with several locations showing slight cooling in this dataset. Because these temperature results change with the analysis window and come from a coarse model-based grid, we present them as findings that need independent validation rather than as conclusions.

Architecture. A Flask backend serves the analysis results as a JSON API. A React, TypeScript, and Tailwind frontend provides the map, charts, and results table. Both parts are deployed on Vercel.

Limitations and next steps. NASA POWER is a roughly 50 km grid, results reflect regional change rather than city-level detail.
details:
What it does. Earth System Trend Detective is an interactive web application that detects and displays long-term environmental change using NASA data. It analyzes monthly temperature and rainfall at 20 locations across north-west India and shows each place on a map, colored by whether its trend is increasing, decreasing, or not statistically significant. Users can switch between temperature and rainfall, change the analysis period, click any location to see its yearly anomaly chart with a fitted trend line, and download the results as a CSV file.

How it works. We retrieve monthly records from NASA POWER through its API, clean the data, and remove the seasonal cycle by subtracting each calendar month’s long-term average. We then average the anomalies for each year and test for a trend using the Mann-Kendall test, with Sen’s slope for the rate of change. A place is labeled as changing only when p is below 0.05, so natural variability is not mistaken for a signal. The results are served by a Flask JSON API and displayed in a React, TypeScript, and Tailwind frontend with an interactive map and charts.

What we found. Using the 2000-2025 analysis, rainfall increased significantly at 17 of 20 locations. No location showed significant warming in this dataset, and 13 showed slight cooling, which we treat as a fragile result that needs independent validation.

Benefits and intended impact. The app makes statistical climate evidence understandable at a glance for students, planners, and the public. In a region where agriculture and water supply depend on rainfall and heat, knowing where change is real, and where it is not, supports better planning and avoids overreaction to noise.

Creativity. Instead of showing only a trend line, the app builds honesty into the interface. We ran the analysis over two time windows (1990-2025 and 2000-2025), and each location carries a Robust flag showing whether its result holds in both. This separates reliable findings from period-dependent ones, and we report the weaker temperature result with appropriate caution.

Factors we considered. We considered the coarse resolution (about 50 km) of the model-based data, the risk of false positives when testing many locations, and the fact that a trend shows that something changed but not why. We kept the method transparent and the design simple, and we list these limits in the app.

Tools. Python (pandas, NumPy, pymannkendall, requests) for analysis; Flask for the API; React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet, and Chart.js for the frontend; NASA POWER as the data source; GitHub and Vercel for hosting. Everything runs in a standard web browser, with no special hardware needed.

Future work. We plan to add NASA satellite products such as vegetation and land surface temperature, validate against station records, and expand to more regions.
